newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Firms await Hungary privatisation jackpot.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Firms await Hungary privatisation jackpot.

text.p: Hungary's state privatisation agency APV is bracing itself for a huge company payout of privatisation revenues as a result of an almost forgotten 1989 law designed to encourage sell-offs.
"We believe we will have to pay out around 30 billion forints ($170 million) and plan to do so by the end of the year," APV spokesman Adam Dudits told Reuters.
The 1989 law promised state-owned companies which transformed themselved into shareholder companies before 1992 that they would receive 20 percent of all subsequent privatisation revenues.

However, despite privatisation revenues thus far of 835 billion forints, ($4.7 billion) the payout obligation was quietly forgotten until chemicals firm TVK signalled its intention in December to claim five billion forints from APV.
Dudits said after talks with TVK it was decided to pay all outstanding arrears.
"APV has decided that every company entitled to repayment will be treated equally," Dudits said. "They will be all paid at the same time in equal instalments as privatisation revenues come in."
Dudits said he could not name other companies qualifying for the payout but analysts believe most of the main listed companies on the Budapest Stock Exchange could be in for a windfall.
"Most of the blue chips are eligible," said Rudi Voros of ICE Securities in London "That includes MOL, Egis, Zalakeramia, Pick and OTP and others."

However Borsodchem, which also became a limited company before 1992, may not qualify because it was under state administration immediately prior to its transformation, when it was restructured and had its debts written off, Voros said.
LOCAL COUNCILS ALSO COMPENSATED

Istvan Racz of CS First Boston in Budapest believes APV, which also plans this year to settle debts with local councils of around 30 billion forints in compensation for privatised assets, will be able to honour its obligations as it has around $3 billion worth of assets it could put on the market.

"Not all of it can be marketed at the same speed but if you exclude assets whose early privatisation may be contentious, we can still talk about some $3 million worth of assets which could be sold off speedily if there is a need for money."
However, Racz believes that due to a general improvement in both government sector finances and the debt burden, the government is less in need of extra revenues to prop up its central budget.
"Debt per GDP is falling and the debt servicing burden is also declining so the government may actually want to keep some of these assets in reserve," he said.
Last month the APV board said it would propose a privatisation revenue target of 180 billion forints ($970 million), which Racz says will enable it to meet all its obligations easily.

"The APV's spending plans on compensation plus restructuring and operational costs would give a total of 100 billion forints and an additional 50 billion forints to be paid to the Treasury for paying government debt," he said.
Racz said the effect on the bourse performance of the companies benefiting from compensation will depend on how much market players have anticipated the additional equity.
"It depends to what extent the market is aware of the money coming and its timing," he said.
Voros said many of the firms in line for a payout were still unaware of the imminent windfall.
"When the TVK news came out, I phoned a few companies and some of then expressed surprise, saying they'd forgotten about it all."
Voros said one fly in the ointment may be a stipulation in the original law that the money must be spent on issuing shares to employees.
Most companies, notably TVK, have almost reached the 10 percent limit set out in their articles on the proportion of their share capital classified as employee shares.
However, Dudits told Reuters APV will be turning a blind eye to this aspect of the law.
"We will give every company the money to which it is entitled and we will not be checking how they spend it," he said.
"It would create such a scandal not to hand over the money I don't think anyone else will be checking either."
